name: Realm

status.note: MongoDB deprecated the Realm SDKs and Atlas Device Sync in September 2024 and shut sync down on 30 September 2025; sync-free community releases of the local database continue.

summary: An embedded object database for mobile apps, a replacement for SQLite and Core Data, whose cloud sync service MongoDB shut down in 2025.
intro: Realm runs inside the app, on a phone, tablet, watch or desktop, and stores objects instead of tables. You declare classes in Swift, Kotlin, C#, JavaScript, Dart or C++, and Realm persists them to a file on the device without an ORM in between. Objects are live: when one is changed anywhere in the app, every reference to it sees the new value, and queries and objects can notify observers, which SwiftUI and other UI frameworks use to redraw. Writes happen in transactions, the file can be encrypted, and because the data is local the app works the same offline.

All the SDKs share one C++ storage engine, Realm Core. Until 2025 they could also connect to MongoDB Atlas Device Sync, which kept the on-device database in sync with a MongoDB Atlas cluster and with other devices, together with App Services sign-in, functions and permission rules.

MongoDB announced in September 2024 that it was deprecating Atlas Device Sync and the Atlas Device SDKs, and on 30 September 2025 sync, App Services authentication and the SDKs reached end of life. MongoDB said the on-device database would continue as an open-source project, and each SDK has a `community` branch with the sync code removed, released for Swift as version 20 (20.0.6 in September 2026). MongoDB engineers still review and release changes, but there is no new feature work, and apps that synced must move to another service.
strengths: Objects map straight to the language’s classes, with no ORM or SQL
Live objects and change notifications that suit reactive UIs such as SwiftUI
Local-first: data is on the device, so apps work offline, and the file can be encrypted
One core engine behind SDKs for Swift, Kotlin, .NET, JavaScript, Dart and C++, under Apache 2.0
limits: Deprecated by MongoDB: no new features, and its future depends on community maintenance
The sync service is gone; apps that relied on Atlas Device Sync or App Services sign-in need a replacement backend
A device-local database, not a server: sharing data between users needs your own API or sync
The file format and APIs are Realm’s own, so moving to SQLite or another store means migrating data and code

goodFor.why: Each SDK runs Realm Core inside the app and persists the app’s own classes to a file on the device, with no server or ORM.

specs.data-model: Objects declared as classes in the app’s language, kept live
specs.transactions: Write transactions on the local file
specs.replication: None since Atlas Device Sync shut down on 30 September 2025
specs.storage-engine: Realm Core, one C++ engine shared by all SDKs, writing a local, optionally encrypted file
specs.deployment: Embedded library; SDKs for Swift, Kotlin, .NET, JavaScript, Dart and C++

story: Alexander Stigsen and Bjarne Christiansen, developers at Nokia in Copenhagen, founded TightDB in 2011 and went through Y Combinator’s summer 2011 batch. Mobile developers then stored data in SQLite or Apple’s Core Data. The company launched publicly as Realm in 2014, pitching its database as a replacement for both, and in March 2015 raised $20 million, saying it ran on more than 100 million devices. The Cocoa and Java SDKs were open source under Apache 2.0, and the core engine was later opened too.

Realm added a sync server and platform for keeping device data in step with a backend. In April 2019 MongoDB agreed to buy Realm for $39 million, citing more than 100,000 active developers and over 2 billion downloads, and sync moved to MongoDB Atlas as Atlas Device Sync, with the SDKs sold as the Atlas Device SDKs.
In September 2024 MongoDB deprecated Device Sync and the SDKs, with end of life on 30 September 2025. The local database lives on in sync-free community branches.

choices.why: App code already works with objects. Persisting the classes themselves removed the mapping layer that SQLite needs and that Core Data adds.
Instead of copying rows into objects that go stale, every reference reads the current data, so UIs can subscribe to changes rather than re-query.
Realm Core, the C++ storage engine, sits under every language SDK, so the same database file and query engine work on iOS, Android, desktop and the server.
